text: There are some who question the relevance of space activities in a developing nation. To us, there is no ambiguity of purpose. We do not have the fantasy of competing with the economically advanced nations in the exploration of the moon or the planets or manned space flight. But we are convinced that if we are to play a meaningful role nationally, and in the community of nations, we must be second to none in the application of advanced technologies to the real problems of man and society, which we find in our country. And we should note that the application of sophisticated technologies and methods of analysis to our problems is not to be confused with embarking on grandiose schemes, whose primary impact is for show rather than for progress measured in hard economic and social terms.
source: Vikram Sarabhai, Speech at the United Nations Conference on the Exploration and Peaceful Uses of Outer Space, 1968

text: The question was frequently asked: why should a developing country like India invest in a space programme when there are pressing needs for food, shelter, and healthcare? My answer has always been the same: it is precisely because of these pressing needs that we cannot afford to ignore the immense potential of space technology. A satellite in orbit can survey our natural resources, predict weather patterns for our farmers, provide communication links to our most remote villages, and broadcast educational programmes to millions simultaneously. No other single investment can yield such transformative returns for a nation of our scale and diversity.
source: Vikram Sarabhai, Address to the Indian Science Congress, 1969

text: India's space programme was born not from a desire to demonstrate technological prowess, but from a deep conviction that space technology could serve as an instrument of national development. When I proposed the establishment of INCOSPAR in 1962, the vision was clear: to develop indigenous capability in satellite technology for applications in communication, meteorology, remote sensing, and education. Every rupee invested in this programme must ultimately improve the life of the common Indian citizen. That is the measure by which we should judge our success.
source: Vikram Sarabhai, Founding Address at INCOSPAR, 1962

text: The establishment of the Indian Space Research Organisation marks a new chapter in our national journey. ISRO is not merely an administrative restructuring of INCOSPAR; it represents a maturation of our ambitions and capabilities. We now have the institutional architecture to pursue satellite development, launch vehicle technology, and ground-based applications with the seriousness and scale they demand. The road ahead is long and arduous, but we have demonstrated through Thumba that determination and scientific rigour can overcome the most daunting constraints.

I have often been asked about the philosophy behind India's approach to space technology. Let me be very clear: we are not interested in space for the sake of space. We are interested in space because of what it can do on the ground. The Satellite Instructional Television Experiment, which we are now planning with NASA, is a perfect embodiment of this philosophy. We will use an American satellite to beam educational television programmes directly to 5,000 Indian villages. This experiment will demonstrate, once and for all, that advanced technology can be a great equaliser, bringing the finest teachers and the most current knowledge to the most remote and underserved communities in our country.
source: Vikram Sarabhai, Speech on SITE Project Planning, 1970

text: The story of Thumba is one that I hold very dear. When we needed a location near the magnetic equator to launch our first sounding rockets, we found it in a small fishing village in Kerala. The local bishop agreed to let us use St. Mary Magdalene Church as our office. The bishop's house became our workshop. The cattle shed became our laboratory. We transported our first rocket on a bicycle. This is not a story of poverty or limitation — it is a story of resourcefulness and determination. It proves that the most advanced scientific work can begin from the humblest of circumstances, provided the vision and the will are strong enough.
source: Vikram Sarabhai, Address to Young Scientists at PRL, 1967

text: The successful launch of our first sounding rocket from Thumba on November 21, 1963, was a moment of profound significance. The Nike-Apache rocket that we launched that day was American-made, and we received generous assistance from NASA. But the importance of that launch was not the rocket itself — it was what it represented. It proved that India could participate in the global scientific enterprise of space research. It gave our young scientists and engineers the confidence that they could master this technology. And it set in motion the process of building indigenous capability that will, in time, free us from dependence on foreign technology.
source: Vikram Sarabhai, Report on First Sounding Rocket Launch, 1963

text: The Thumba Equatorial Rocket Launching Station is strategically located near the magnetic equator, making it ideal for studying the equatorial ionosphere and the phenomenon of equatorial electrojet. Our sounding rocket programme has already yielded valuable scientific data on cosmic rays, upper atmospheric composition, and meteorological phenomena. But beyond the science, Thumba has become a training ground for our engineers and technicians. Every launch teaches us something new about propulsion, telemetry, tracking, and range safety. This cumulative learning is what will enable us to eventually build our own rockets and satellites.

The decision to dedicate the Thumba Equatorial Rocket Launching Station to the United Nations in 1968 was guided by a simple principle: science knows no borders. By making Thumba available to the international scientific community, we are not giving away our advantage — we are strengthening it. International cooperation brings access to the best minds, the latest techniques, and shared resources. India's position as a responsible participant in the global scientific community is enhanced, not diminished, by such gestures of openness.
source: Vikram Sarabhai, UN Dedication Ceremony Speech, 1968

text: Our satellite programme must be designed with India's specific needs in mind. A communication satellite system for India is not a luxury — it is a necessity. Consider the geography: a vast subcontinent with mountain ranges, deserts, dense forests, and thousands of islands. Building terrestrial communication networks to connect every village would take decades and cost astronomical sums. A satellite system can achieve in years what conventional infrastructure would take generations to accomplish. This is what I mean by leapfrogging — using the most advanced technology to bypass the slow, incremental path of development.
source: Vikram Sarabhai, Proposal for Indian National Satellite System, 1970
